column1: # THE FLEET. One row per class, smallest to largest. Tab separated, so a blurb can hold commas and
# apostrophes freely. Edit here (or in a spreadsheet, exported as TSV), then:
#     npm run import && npm run catalogue
# Lines starting with # are ignored, so notes and section breaks are fine.
# THE GAMEPLAY COLUMNS. These are what the fight and the shipyard read.
# active      yes if she is in the game. Anything else, blank included, lays her up: her row stays
#             here with her figures as they stood and she comes back the day the column says yes.
#             So the table is the fleet's whole history and the game is the part of it at sea, and a
#             class rebuilt keeps her old row beside her new one. That is why two rows may share an
#             id, as long as only one of them sails.
# id          a short camelCase name, unique among the ships that sail. Becomes the key everything
#             else refers to, so renaming one is retiring a ship and commissioning another.
# name        what a captain reads. No em dashes, no interpuncts. The fleet's own names are written
#             as the captain who drew up the table wrote them, capitals and all, which is why the
#             sentence-case rule that governs the rest of the game's copy stops at this column.
# price       coins to buy the bare hull. 0 for the ship she starts with.
# hull, crew  maximum health in the same points the bars already use. Hull is the reference's own
#             timber formula; crew is her battle complement, floored at 25 because a crew bar is a
#             health bar and a dozen points is four musket balls.
# speed       her own pace before a stitch of canvas, off her working speed under sail.
# hand        how she answers her rudder, before canvas. From the reference's handling components
#             less the rig and the crew: her sails carry the rig half themselves.
# canvas      how much sail she WANTS to get moving, as displacement to the two thirds. The most
#             important number here: it is why a half-rigged big ship is genuinely bad, and why the
#             same suit drives a cutter hard.
# tons        the weight of iron she can bear, in the same tons her guns are weighed in: a full
#             battery of the gun she was built around, both sides, plus her chasers and her rail.
#             It is a real limit rather than a penalty. The shipyard steps her battery down a grade
#             at a time until it fits under this, so a raft cannot mount thirty-six pounders, and
#             what she does carry costs her in handling in proportion to how close to it she is.
# broadside   guns A SIDE, mirrored, because that is how a volley fires: one gun bought is one gun
#             each side and two aboard.
# bow         chasers on her bow. A total rather than a side, because she has only the one bow.
# swivel      swivels on her rails, and a total as well. They fire in the volley with her muskets.
# masts       where she can step one, "station/size", space separated, bow aft.
#             stations: bowsprit fore main mizzen bonaventure
#             sizes:    boat small medium large heavy
#             The bowsprit takes a SPAR rather than a mast, which is what her headsails hang on.
# bowsprit    yes or no. Whether she carries the spar at all.
# blurb       one line a captain reads. May be left empty.
# A BLANK IN speed, hand, canvas OR tons IS NOT A DERIVATION. Each falls back to 1, which describes
# a quick, handy, easily driven ship that can carry nothing, and is right for no class above a boat.
# Fill them in. Every other gameplay column has to be filled as well.
# THE REFERENCE COLUMNS. Everything from `era` rightward is what the class WAS rather than what she
# does in a fight: no fight reads any of it, `npm run import` writes it to src/shipref.js, and
# `hullform.js` is the one reader. The fourteen marked (drawn) are how she is DRAWN, in the menu
# model and at sea. The rest are recorded for whoever comes to refine her form and are read by
# nothing yet, which is not the same as being free to invent: a wrong figure here is a wrong hull
# the day somebody does read it.
# Lengths are feet and weights are tons. bowFine, tumblehome, deadrise, sheer and castle are 1 to 5
# judgement scores, 1 for least and 5 for most.
# era         the years she was in service, written as a range. Text rather than a number.
# region      where she was built and sailed.
# role        what she was for.
# lod         (drawn) length on deck, feet. With beam, how big she is drawn in both views. Sizes are
#             compressed around the galleon, so twice the length is not twice the ship on screen.
# lbp         length between perpendiculars, feet. The measured length, shorter than on deck.
# beam        (drawn) extreme breadth, feet. Her drawn width, and with her length her collision
#             ellipse in a fight.
# draft       how deep she floats, feet.
# depth       depth of hold, feet: keelson to the deck above it.
# freeboard   (drawn) height of side above the water amidships, feet. The depth of side in the model.
# lb          length to beam, as a ratio. High is long and lean, low is short and beamy.
# bd          beam to depth, as a ratio. High is shallow and beamy, low is deep and narrow.
# burthen     builder's old measurement tons: what she was rated to carry.
# disp        displacement, tons: what she actually weighs afloat.
# bowFine     (drawn) how fine her entry is. 5 is a clipper's bow and 1 a carrack's. It narrows her
#             bow and pulls her shoulders aft.
# tumblehome  (drawn) how far her sides roll inward above the waterline. 5 is a fluyt.
# deadrise    how sharply her bottom rises from the keel. 1 is a flat floor.
# sheer       (drawn) how much her deck sweeps up towards bow and stern.
# castle      (drawn) how built up her ends are. 1 is an open boat, 2 raises a quarterdeck, 3 and up
#             add a forecastle. It is also what a windowed stern needs before it shows any lights.
# stern       (drawn) the shape of her stern, as one of the named types. Scow, Round, Pear,
#             Elliptical, Raking transom, Overhanging and Square each have geometry of their own,
#             and any other name draws a plain transom, which is what Transom and Gallery do. A name
#             holding "gallery" or "castle" lights her stern windows if her castle is 3 or more.
# mastHeight  (drawn) how tall her rig stands, as a multiple of the galleon's. Scales her masts in
#             both views.
# decks       how many of her decks carry guns: 1, 1-2, 2, 2-3 or 3. Text, because a range is not a
#             number. Recorded description now: `battery` says deck by deck where her guns actually
#             stood, and that is what her ports are drawn from.
# wale        the thickness of her main wale, inches: the heavy belt of timber along her side.
# topside     the thickness of her topside planking, inches.
# roomSpace   (drawn) room and space, feet: from one frame to the next. A gunport was framed on it,
#             running a little over one space wide, so this is the size of every port she shows.
# species     (drawn) what she was built of, which is also her colour: Oak, Live oak, Teak, Cedar or
#             Pine. Any other name is painted as oak.
# timber      (drawn) how dense that timber is, oak being 1. Denser timber reads a little darker.
# crewMin     the fewest hands she could be worked with, as against the battle complement in `crew`.
# cruise      her everyday speed, knots.
# topSpeed    the best she was ever driven, knots.
# manoeuvre   how handy she was, 0 to 100. The reference's own score, and what `hand` came out of.
# histGuns    (drawn) how many guns she really carried, of every sort. Half of them is exactly her
#             `broadside` bearing for every class in the fleet, which is how the ports and the guns
#             that fire out of them agree without the catalogue and the reference ever meeting.
#             `battery` says where those guns stood and has to add up to this.
# battery     (drawn) her establishment, deck by deck, as guns aboard rather than a side. Gun decks
#             first and lowest deck first, then what she carried on her upper works after a plus:
#             "10" is a cutter's ten on one open deck, "28+8/2" a frigate with a gun deck of 28 and
#             ten more on her quarterdeck and forecastle, "28/28/30+12/2" a first rate. The figures
#             sum to histGuns and every gun deck takes an even number, half of them a side.
#             A GUN DECK AND AN UPPER WORKS ARE NOT THE SAME FITTING, which is the whole reason this
#             column exists. A gun deck is a continuous battery pierced through her side, so its
#             ports run the length of her, under the castles the way a lower deck really did. Her
#             quarterdeck and forecastle guns stood in the open behind a bulwark, with no lidded
#             port to show, and drawn as such they are what leaves a two-decker's waist empty.
#             After the plus, two figures are the quarterdeck and the forecastle in that order, with
#             her waist bare between them. One figure is a battery that ran the whole length of her
#             upper works, which is what a spar-decked heavy frigate had. Write "2/0" rather than
#             "2" for a ship who carried hers aft only.
#             A BOAT IS NOT PIERCED AT ALL. A lidded port is cut through her topside under the deck
#             above it, and a hull with a castle score of 1 has neither, so her whole battery is
#             drawn standing at her rail however this column is written.

column16: A raft with a mast and one gun. She floats, she fires, and she is yours.

column16: A single mast on a hull with some beam under it. She answers the helm sweetly.

column16: Broad, deep and stiff, with more sail than a boat her size has any right to.

column1: yes
column16: Two raked masts on a hull cut like a knife. She outruns ships that outgun her.

column1: yes
column16: Square on the fore and fore and aft on the main. She will do most things well enough.

column1: yes
column16: Long, low and lateen rigged, with a crew that would rather board you than shoot.

column1: yes
column16: Three masts and one flush deck of guns. The smallest ship that looks like a warship.

column1: yes
column16: Rated at last, and the smallest thing a post captain will admit to commanding.

column1: yes
column16: The same corsair hull grown a third mast and a great many more men.

column1: yes
column16: A whole deck of eighteens and the legs to choose her own fight.

column1: yes
column16: Live oak frames set close enough that round shot comes off her sides.

column1: yes
column16: Two decks of guns on a hull too slow to run and too light for the line.

column1: yes
column16: Sixty four guns, and the smallest ship anyone will put in the line of battle.
